rationale: Eight of eleven historical Parkinsonian cases had tremor. Injected drug in oil and wax and oral belladonna lowered amplitude without materially changing incidence or rate. No oil-only exposure. The 1951 Ebin review is the same study family.

The 200-person clinical series covered several diagnoses. The author describes possible relief of painful rigidity with the injected drug and gives no individual tremor estimate or oil-only comparison.
Three of six animals received the drug dissolved in injected peanut oil. The reported effect is on levodopa-induced dyskinesia. Rest tremor appears in model description without an oil-only contrast.

Both diets contained peanut oil. The low rod yielded longer retention under the low-alpha-linolenic acid diet, the high rod and traction comparisons were inconclusive or unchanged, and some learning measures were weaker. No resting-tremor assessment.
The peanut-plus-rapeseed blend was the comparison for salmon-palm oil, with several dietary fatty acids changing. The fish-oil blend reduced general activity or changed habituation.

Six of sixty participants with peanut allergy reported reactions after crude oil, including two observable or measurable reactions. None reacted after the refined oil. Outcomes are acute allergy signs, with no identifiable rest-tremor response.

One trial assigned 129 healthy adults to eight weeks of peanut, olive, safflower oil or no study oil. The analyzed denominator for the activity result is unverified. Its companion paper reports no significant change in general activity, and neither report assessed tremor.
Measured fatty acids, tocopherols and phytosterols in specified cold-pressed oil. Availability of measured composition supplies no observed symptom contrast.
The table associates peanut-oil massage with infantile paralysis. This row identifies no direct witness, measured response or comparable oral route.
Table 2 records customary cooking and topical uses. Study citation counts measure use reports and cannot establish response or clinical effect.
The combined methanolic almond, peanut and watermelon seed extract favored less block catalepsy and greater activity. It did not test peanut oil, an isolated seed arm or a resting-tremor outcome.

The main report identifies oil-based control spread in healthy adults and tests cognition, stress and mood. Registration and later companion outcomes belong to the same intervention. No distinct oil-free comparator or tremor endpoint.

The ENHANce trial and nested TEMPUS-FUGIT use a peanut-oil omega-3 placebo in older adults with sarcopenia. The protocol and feasibility report address physical function, and the family has no separate Parkinson tremor result.
Metformin-treated outpatients consumed dietary oils including groundnut. The reported glucose and lipid outcomes do not record tremor or an acute hypoglycemic movement phenotype.
